title: Two surfaces, one magnetic circulation
focus: Follow the fields through a charging circuit
text: Picture a capacitor being charged. Current flows in the wire, but no conduction charge crosses the vacuum gap. Now draw a loop around the wire. A flat surface through that loop cuts the wire. A curved surface with the same edge can pass through the gap instead. Can these surfaces give two different values for the same magnetic circulation? This puzzle takes us from Maxwell's equations all the way to an optical coating.

title: Keep the boundary fixed
focus: One loop can bound many oriented surfaces
text: The magnetic circulation is an integral along the loop. It has one value once we fix the direction of travel. Match each surface normal to that direction by the right hand rule. Ampere's original magnetostatic equation counts the conduction current through the surface. The wire surface counts current. The gap surface does not. A charging circuit lies outside the assumptions of magnetostatics.

title: Predict the missing term
focus: What counts across a vacuum gap?
text: Pause and choose. In the ideal vacuum gap, is the electric flux fixed, does it change so that epsilon zero times its rate of change equals the lead current, or do electrons carry that current through the vacuum? Sketch the two surfaces before choosing. Think about what happens to the charge on the plates during charging.

title: The changing flux closes the budget
focus: Same circulation, different contributions
text: The changing flux supplies the missing term. In the parallel plate approximation, the electric flux across the gap is the plate charge divided by epsilon zero. Differentiate with respect to time. The result, multiplied by epsilon zero, is the rate at which charge arrives. Maxwell's correction makes the surface choice consistent. Displacement current has units of amperes. In this gap it describes a changing field without a flow of charge carriers.

title: A changing magnetic field drives circulation
focus: Induction exists with or without a wire loop
text: Now drive current up a long solenoid. Take the magnetic field inside to point along positive z and grow steadily. Outside, approximate the magnetic field as zero. Place an imaginary circle around the coil, without adding a conductor. Faraday's law relates the electric circulation around that circle to the rate of change of magnetic flux through its disk.

title: Flux depends on the field-filled area
focus: Inside the coil, use πr². Outside, use πa².
text: Cylindrical symmetry makes the induced electric field azimuthal in this idealization. The disk flux uses only the part of the disk where the magnetic field exists. For a circle inside the coil, that area grows as radius squared. Outside the coil, it saturates at the coil's cross section. The circumference keeps growing, however. Divide the rate of flux change by that circumference.

title: A field can circulate where its curl vanishes
focus: Clockwise outside, with magnitude proportional to 1/r
text: The electric field points clockwise. Positive flux increases, so circulation is negative for the counterclockwise orientation. Beyond the coil radius, its magnitude decreases inversely with radius. The field can be nonzero even where its local curl vanishes. Outside the coil, a spanning disk for a loop encircling the axis also includes the interior. This distinction between local and integral statements is worth slowing down for.

title: From local rotation to a boundary integral
focus: Stokes' theorem connects a surface and its edge
text: Curl measures circulation per area in the small-loop limit. To see how local curls build up, imagine tiling a disk with tiny oriented loops. On shared edges, neighboring loops traverse the same edge in opposite directions. Those contributions cancel. Summing all of the little loops leaves circulation along the outside boundary.

title: Shrink a loop without crossing the coil
focus: A small loop can sit entirely in the exterior
text: Take a tiny disk in the exterior that does not enclose the solenoid. Its normal is still along positive z. The changing magnetic flux through that disk is zero in this model. Yet a probe at a point on the disk detects a nonzero induced electric field. A curl measurement compares contributions around the whole small loop. It is different from a point measurement of the field.

title: Use orientation consistently
focus: Reverse both the normal and the traversal direction
text: The small-loop circulation vanishes. The field contributions cancel in the line integral. In differential form, the curl of the electric field equals minus the time derivative of the magnetic field. Integrate this relation over the oriented surface, then apply Stokes' theorem. Reversing the chosen normal reverses the loop direction and both sides change sign together.

title: Charge has a local budget
focus: Outward current flux lowers charge in a fixed volume
text: Charge conservation gives a useful diagnostic. Choose a fixed volume. Count the charge inside, and count the current leaving through its closed surface. If more charge flows out than in, the stored charge falls. The divergence theorem converts the outward flux into a volume integral of the divergence. Since the choice of volume is arbitrary, we obtain the local continuity equation.

title: A varying current density can be divergence-free
focus: Compare net flux, not just arrow lengths
text: In a straight steady conductor that narrows, the same current passes through every cross section, while the average current density increases in the narrow section. A plot of that axial average can slope upward. It is not the three-dimensional divergence. Near a taper the current field can have transverse components, and an insulating wall contributes no outward charge flux.

title: Continuity also checks Maxwell's correction
focus: The divergence of a curl is zero
text: The net flux is zero. The same current enters and leaves, so charge does not accumulate. Now take the divergence of the Ampere-Maxwell equation. The divergence of the left hand curl vanishes identically. Gauss's law turns the divergence of the changing electric field term into the time derivative of charge density. What remains on the right is the continuity equation.

title: Follow energy through the gap
focus: The Poynting vector points across the side boundary

title: Balance flux against field energy
focus: Poynting's theorem connects fields and matter
text: Poynting's theorem follows by dotting the curl equations with the appropriate fields and using the divergence identity for a cross product. The result separates the rate of change of field energy, the outward energy flux and the rate at which fields do work on matter. In the vacuum gap, the work term is zero. For this quasistatic example, the leading change is the electric energy.

title: The inward power equals V times I
focus: Flux balance in the ideal parallel-plate limit
text: The outward power is negative. Integrate the radial Poynting flux over the cylindrical side. Using the Ampere-Maxwell field at the rim, the inward power is voltage times current. Independently, differentiate one half times capacitance times voltage squared. It gives the same power. In the lab you will check both calculations and estimate when neglecting changing magnetic energy and edge fringing is reasonable.

title: At an interface, match both tangential fields
focus: Normal incidence, real impedances, no surface sheet current
text: Move from slowly changing fields to a traveling plane wave. Its electric and magnetic fields are transverse. The ratio of electric field to magnetic field intensity is the wave impedance. At a plane interface, match tangential electric and magnetic fields. For the reflected wave the magnetic field changes sign relative to the electric field, because the propagation direction reverses.

title: Amplitudes and powers are different
focus: Use impedance when converting fields to flux
text: Take two linear lossless nonmagnetic media. The impedance is the vacuum impedance divided by refractive index. A transmitted amplitude of one half, for example, does not by itself tell you the fraction of power transmitted.

title: Add a layer and track propagation phase

Impedance sets the amplitude matching.
